text: Joab son of Zeruiah realized that the king's heart was turning toward Absalom.

So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman, and told her to pretend to be in mourning, putting on mourning clothes and not using any oil, acting like a woman who had been grieving a long time for someone dead.
He told her to go to the king and speak to him along the lines he gave her, and he put the words in her mouth.
So the woman from Tekoa went to the king, fell on her face to the ground, paid homage, and cried out that the king should help her.
The king asked what was troubling her, and she said she was indeed a widow, since her husband had died.
She said her servant had two sons, and the two of them got into a fight out in the field where there was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him.

Now, she said, the whole family had risen up against her, telling her to hand over the one who struck his brother so they could put him to death for the life of the brother he killed, even though that would destroy the heir too, extinguishing the last ember she had left and leaving her husband no name or descendant on the earth.
The king told the woman to go home, and he would issue a command on her behalf.
The woman from Tekoa told the king that the guilt would rest on her and her father's house, and the king and his throne would be innocent.
The king said that if anyone spoke against her, she should bring them to him, and they would not bother her again.

Then she asked him to invoke the LORD his God, so that the avenger of blood would not increase the ruin and destroy her son; and he said, as surely as the LORD lives, not one hair of your son will fall to the ground.
Then the woman asked to speak one more word to the king, and he told her to speak.
She asked why then he had planned such a thing against God's people, since by not bringing back his own banished son, the king was, in effect, pronouncing himself guilty.

She said that they all must die eventually, like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up again, and that God does not take away life but instead devises ways so that the banished one need not remain estranged from him.

She explained that the reason she had come to say this to the king was that the people had made her afraid, and she thought she should speak to the king, since perhaps he would grant his servant's request.
She said the king would surely listen and rescue his servant from the hand of anyone who wanted to cut off both her and her son from God's inheritance.
She added that she hoped the king's word would now bring her comfort, since the king was like an angel of God in discerning good and evil, and asked that the LORD his God be with him.
The king answered the woman by asking her not to hide from him anything he asked; and she said, let my lord the king speak.

The king asked whether Joab's hand was behind all this, and the woman answered that as surely as the king lived, no one could turn to the right or the left from anything the king had said, since it was indeed his servant Joab who had commanded her and put all these words in her mouth.
She said Joab had done this to bring about a change in the situation, and that the king's wisdom was like the wisdom of the angel of God, knowing everything that happens in the land.
Then the king told Joab that he would do this thing, and instructed him to go and bring back the young man Absalom.
Joab fell to the ground on his face, paid homage, blessed the king, and said that today he knew he had found favor in the king's sight, since the king had granted his servant's request.
So Joab got up, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.
But the king said Absalom could go to his own house and not come into the king's presence, so Absalom went to his own house and did not see the king's face.
Now in all Israel there was no one as praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom; from the sole of his foot to the top of his head there was no blemish in him.
Whenever he cut the hair of his head, which he did every year since it grew too heavy for him, he would weigh it, and it weighed two hundred shekels by the royal standard.
Three sons were born to Absalom, and one daughter named Tamar, who was a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem without seeing the king's face.
Then Absalom sent for Joab to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him, and when he sent a second time, Joab still would not come.
So Absalom told his servants to go set Joab's barley field, which was next to his own, on fire, and Absalom's servants set the field on fire.
Then Joab got up, went to Absalom's house, and asked why his servants had set his field on fire.

Absalom told Joab that he had sent word asking him to come so he could send him to the king to ask why he had been brought back from Geshur at all — it would have been better if he had just stayed there — and now he wanted to see the king's face, and if there was guilt in him, let the king put him to death.
So Joab went to the king and told him, and the king summoned Absalom, who came to the king and bowed down with his face to the ground before him, and the king kissed Absalom.
